title: Units Digits & Cycles
coreInsight: The last digits of repeated powers often form periodic residue cycles, so a huge exponent can be replaced by its position in a short cycle.
targetLearnerRealization: The units digit of repeated powers follows a cycle, so a huge exponent only determines a position within that short cycle.
learningObjectives: Generate and verify a units-digit cycle by repeated multiplication modulo 10.
Reduce a large exponent to a correctly indexed cycle position.
Handle remainder zero as the final slot of a one-indexed power cycle.
Track and combine separate cycles in sums of powers.

continuity.openingCallback: Treat each units digit as a remainder modulo 10 and watch repeated multiplication revisit earlier positions.
closingSeeds: A short periodic state can replace a huge repeated computation in many sequence problems.

misconceptionTargets.misconception: The cycle length can be assumed without checking.
Cycle positions are indexed from zero in every setup.
Every base has the same cycle length.
The exponent itself is the units digit pattern.

beats.purpose: Create the need for a units-digit cycle from an impossibly large direct power.
beats.expectedRealization: Only the base's units digit matters, and successive powers of 3 repeat 3,9,7,1 every four exponents.
beats.transitionIn: A units digit is a remainder modulo 10. Compute only that remainder as the power grows, rather than the full number.
beats.transitionOut: The fifth units digit returned to 3, verifying a four-step cycle; exponent 2012 completed whole cycles and landed on 1.
beats.whyNow: The approved anchor creates an authentic large-exponent obstacle that dissolves as soon as the cycle is discovered.
beats.entryBridge: Replace 13 by its units digit 3, then multiply by 3 repeatedly and reduce modulo 10 after each step.
beats.exitBridge: Divide the exponent by the verified cycle length and interpret remainder zero as a completed cycle.
beats.reusedRepresentation: A four-position cycle ring labeled by successive units digits.
learnerPrompts: What repeats even though the full powers grow?
Which next value confirms the cycle has closed?
Where does exponent 2012 land in a four-position cycle?
beats.incorrectFeedback: Generate 3,9,7,1, confirm the next value is 3, then use 2012 mod 4.

steps.body: Since 13≡3 (mod 10), the powers of 13 have the same units digits as powers of 3.
Repeated multiplication gives 3,9,7,1, then returns to 3, so the verified cycle length is 4.
2012 = 4×503 has remainder 0, which means the final slot of a complete cycle: units digit 1.

resolution.takeaway: A huge exponent becomes a small cycle-position calculation after the cycle is verified.

beats.purpose: Distinguish observed values from a verified repeating cycle.
beats.expectedRealization: The next state is determined by the current units digit, so returning to the starting state guarantees repetition from there.
beats.transitionIn: Seeing four values is not yet proof of the cycle length; compute the next transition.
beats.prompt: Why does the next units digit 1×3→3 verify that 3,9,7,1 will repeat?

options.text: The units digit 3 is the starting state again, and multiplying by 3 determines the same next state 9.
Every power cycle automatically has length 4.
The full value of 3⁵ equals 3.
Four examples are always enough to prove repetition.

beats.correctFeedback: Exactly—the process is deterministic, so returning to the same state forces the same future transitions.
beats.incorrectFeedback: The next units digit depends only on the current units digit and the fixed multiplier 3.

steps.body: From any current units digit u, the next is the units digit of 3u. Once u returns to 3, every later step repeats the earlier path.

resolution.takeaway: Verify a cycle by returning to a previous state under the same transition rule.

beats.purpose: Repair the off-by-one interpretation of a zero cycle remainder.
beats.expectedRealization: Power exponent 1 occupies slot 1, so an exponent divisible by cycle length occupies the final slot, not slot 1.
beats.transitionIn: The cycle lists powers starting at exponent 1, not exponent 0.
beats.prompt: In the cycle [3,9,7,1] for exponents 1,2,3,4, where does exponent 20 land?

options.text: Slot 4, value 1, because 20 completes five full cycles.
Slot 1, value 3, because the remainder is 0.
A nonexistent slot 0.
The units digit is the exponent's units digit 0.

beats.correctFeedback: Right—remainder zero means the end of a complete one-indexed cycle.
beats.incorrectFeedback: Write the first cycle under exponents 1,2,3,4 and continue with exponent 5 returning to slot 1.

steps.body: 20 = 4×5, so exponent 20 is the fourth step of the fifth cycle. Its units digit is 1.

resolution.takeaway: For powers indexed from 1, remainder 0 selects the last cycle slot.

beats.purpose: Show that cycle length depends on the base's units digit.
beats.expectedRealization: Bases ending in 5 stabilize immediately, 9 alternates, and 2 follows a four-step cycle.
beats.transitionIn: Repeat the same cycle-building process for other starting units digits rather than borrowing length 4.

options.text: 5 has cycle [5] of length 1; 9 has [9,1] of length 2; 2 has [2,4,8,6] of length 4.
Every units digit has cycle length 4.
The exponent determines the cycle length.
The full base, not its units digit, determines unrelated cycles.

beats.correctFeedback: Correct—cycle lengths differ and must be generated and verified.
beats.incorrectFeedback: Multiply each current units digit by its fixed base digit until the starting state returns.

visual.ariaLabel: Units-digit cycles of bases ending in five, nine, and two

resolution.takeaway: Discover and verify the cycle for the actual base digit; do not assume a universal length.

beats.purpose: Name the cycle-position method after the anchor and its safeguards.
beats.expectedRealization: Units digits are powers modulo 10, and exponent reduction is valid only after a period is verified.
beats.transitionIn: The repeated states and the exponent's position now form a reusable technique.
beats.name: Units-digit cycle method
beats.conciseDefinition: Reduce the base modulo 10, generate powers until the starting state returns, then reduce the exponent by the verified cycle length.
beats.formalization: If uₙ is the units digit of aⁿ and period L is verified, then uₙ depends on n mod L, with remainder 0 selecting slot L.
beats.memoryHook: Reduce the base, build the loop, locate the exponent.

beats.purpose: Separate the exponent from the units-digit pattern and justify base reduction.
beats.expectedRealization: Bases congruent modulo 10 generate identical units-digit power sequences.
beats.transitionIn: The full base can also be replaced by its remainder position before cycling.
beats.prompt: Why do 47ⁿ and 7ⁿ always have the same units digit for positive integer n?

options.text: 47≡7 (mod 10), and multiplying congruent residues preserves congruence.
47 and 7 are equal numbers.
The exponent itself supplies the units digit.
Every base has the same cycle.

beats.correctFeedback: Exactly—complete tens never affect the remainder modulo 10, even through repeated multiplication.
beats.incorrectFeedback: Replace 47 by its standard remainder 7 modulo 10 before each multiplication.

resolution.takeaway: The base's units digit generates the pattern; the exponent selects a position in it.

beats.purpose: Make the deterministic state transition explicit for arbitrary units cycles.
beats.expectedRealization: Each next units digit is obtained by multiplying the current digit by the fixed base digit and reducing modulo 10.
beats.transitionIn: A cycle is generated locally, one state from the previous one.
beats.prompt: The units digits of powers of 7 begin 7,9,3. What must the next units digit be?

options.text: 1, because 3×7 ends in 1.
4, because every cycle has four distinct digits.
7, because the exponent is 4.
21, without reducing to a units digit.

beats.correctFeedback: Right—multiply the current state by 7 and reduce modulo 10.
beats.incorrectFeedback: The current units digit is 3; calculate the units digit of 3×7.

steps.body: 3×7 = 21 gives next state 1. One more step gives 1×7→7, confirming [7,9,3,1].

resolution.takeaway: The next state comes from the current state, not directly from the exponent's digits.

beats.purpose: Track two power cycles and combine their final residues.
beats.expectedRealization: Both bases reduce to 9; odd powers end in 9; their sum ends in 8.
beats.transitionIn: Two large powers can be reduced independently, then their small residues can be combined.
beats.transitionOut: Both odd exponents selected 9; adding 9+9=18 produced units digit 8.
beats.whyNow: The approved transfer tests separate cycle tracking followed by modular addition without additional prerequisite load.
beats.entryBridge: Reduce both bases to units digit 9, verify the two-step cycle [9,1], and classify each exponent as odd or even.
beats.exitBridge: Add the selected units digits and reduce the sum modulo 10.
beats.reusedRepresentation: Two short cycle rows whose selected positions feed a sum.
learnerPrompts: What units digit replaces each base?
Which slot does each odd exponent select?
What is the units digit of the resulting sum?
beats.correctFeedback: Correct—both powers end in 9, so the sum ends in 8.
beats.incorrectFeedback: The cycle of 9 is [9,1]. Exponents 19 and 99 are both odd.

steps.body: Both 19 and 99 are congruent to 9 modulo 10.
Powers of 9 alternate 9,1. Both exponents are odd, so both powers end in 9.

resolution.takeaway: Track each power's cycle position independently, then combine and reduce the selected residues.

beats.purpose: Assess a four-step cycle with nonzero remainder.
beats.expectedRealization: Twenty-three selects slot 3 of [7,9,3,1], giving units digit 3.
beats.transitionIn: Build and use a four-step cycle without supplied positions.
beats.whyNow: A near item checks the full method independently.
beats.entryBridge: Generate the powers of 7 modulo 10 until 7 returns.
beats.exitBridge: Map the exponent remainder to a one-indexed slot.

steps.body: The cycle is [7,9,3,1]. Since 23=4×5+3, select slot 3, which is 3.

resolution.takeaway: A nonzero exponent remainder names the matching one-indexed slot.

beats.purpose: Assess a cycle of length one.
beats.expectedRealization: Every positive power of a number ending in 6 also ends in 6.
beats.transitionIn: Use the shortest possible verified cycle.
beats.transitionOut: Multiplying a units digit 6 by 6 returns to 6 immediately.
beats.whyNow: A near item prevents automatic use of cycle length four.
beats.exitBridge: The starting state returns after one transition.
beats.incorrectFeedback: Since 6×6 ends in 6, the cycle [6] repeats for every positive exponent.

steps.body: The first units digit is 6, and the next is also 6. Thus the verified period is 1 and 6¹⁰⁰ ends in 6.

resolution.takeaway: Some base digits stabilize rather than moving through four positions.

beats.purpose: Assess exponent reduction without confusing exponent digits and cycle values.
beats.expectedRealization: Fifty selects slot 2 of [3,9,7,1], giving units digit 9.
beats.transitionIn: Separate the exponent remainder 2 from the cycle value stored at slot 2.
beats.transitionOut: The remainder names a position; the value at that position is 9.
beats.whyNow: A mixed item targets the exponent-versus-pattern misconception.
beats.entryBridge: Reduce 50 modulo the verified cycle length 4.
beats.exitBridge: Read the cycle entry rather than reporting the remainder itself.

steps.body: The cycle has length 4 and 50=4×12+2. The second cycle value is 9.

resolution.takeaway: The exponent remainder is an index, not usually the units digit itself.

beats.purpose: Assess two independent four-cycles followed by addition.
beats.expectedRealization: At exponent 31, powers of 2 end in 8 and powers of 3 end in 7, so the sum ends in 5.
beats.transitionIn: Coordinate two different cycles at the same exponent.
beats.transitionOut: Both use exponent slot 3, but the cycle values differ; 8+7 ends in 5.
beats.whyNow: A mixed item ensures shared cycle length is not mistaken for shared values.
beats.entryBridge: Build each base's cycle and reduce 31 modulo 4.
beats.exitBridge: Add the selected units digits and reduce again.
learnerPrompts: What value is in slot 3 of each cycle?
What is the units digit of their sum?

steps.body: Slot 3 gives 8 for powers of 2 and 7 for powers of 3. Their sum 15 has units digit 5.

resolution.takeaway: Cycle position can match while cycle values differ; combine values only after each lookup.

beats.purpose: Assess reducing an exponent expression by the outer cycle length.
beats.expectedRealization: The exponent 2²⁰ is divisible by 4, so it selects the final value 1 in the powers-of-7 cycle.
beats.transitionIn: For the final challenge, the exponent is itself a large power, but only its remainder modulo four is needed.
beats.transitionOut: Since 2²⁰ contains at least two factors of 2, it completes whole four-step cycles and selects 1.
beats.whyNow: The challenge composes exponent reduction with a nested power without evaluating the exponent.
beats.entryBridge: Find the outer units-digit cycle first, then reduce the exponent expression modulo its length.
beats.exitBridge: Interpret remainder zero as the final one-indexed slot.
learnerPrompts: What cycle length governs powers of 7?
Which slot does remainder zero select?
beats.incorrectFeedback: Powers of 7 follow [7,9,3,1]; 2²⁰ is divisible by 4.

steps.body: The verified cycle for 7 is [7,9,3,1] with length 4.
Because 2²⁰ is divisible by 4, the exponent remainder is 0, selecting the fourth slot: units digit 1.

resolution.takeaway: Reduce the exponent expression only as far as the outer cycle requires.

beats.purpose: Consolidate verification, indexing, variable cycle length, and residue lookup.
beats.expectedRealization: A correct units-digit solution distinguishes cycle generation, exponent indexing, and the final cycle value.
beats.transitionIn: Every successful solution followed the same safeguards before reading a digit.
beats.prompt: Which checks belong in a reliable units-digit cycle solution? Select all four.

options.text: Reduce the base modulo 10.
Generate states until a repeated state verifies the cycle.
Map the exponent remainder to the correct one-indexed slot.
Report the cycle value in that slot, then reduce any final operation.
Assume every cycle has length 4.

response.feedback: Reduce, verify, index carefully, and read the stored cycle value.

beats.correctFeedback: Exactly—those four steps avoid the common cycle traps.
beats.incorrectFeedback: Cycle length depends on the base digit and must be verified.

resolution.takeaway: Reduce the base, verify the loop, locate the exponent, and read the cycle value.

beats.purpose: Connect units-digit cycles to broader periodic-sequence reasoning.
beats.expectedRealization: Once a deterministic finite state repeats, all future states repeat and large indices can be reduced by the period.
beats.transitionIn: The powers were enormous, but their modulo-10 state space had only ten possible positions.
beats.prompt: What other repeated process could be simplified by recording a small state, detecting its first verified return, and locating a large index inside the resulting period?
beats.takeaway: Finite deterministic states turn many long computations into short cycle-position problems.
